title: Reimagine Your Temperament
hook: A storm limb photo is open beside a tree-risk tablet. A label stops being destiny when behavior answers back.
counterintuition: The trap is not having a temperament; it is treating a temperament label as permission to repeat the same drift. The sharper move is to choose one behavior that proves a different self-story while the old label is still talking.
tryThisNow: Replace one 'I am just the kind of person who...' sentence with one observable action you will take in the next block.
keyTakeaway: Stop treating distractibility as a fixed identity and choose the next behavior that proves a different self-story so prior intent beats the nearest convincing escape.

The danger with temperament language is that it can sound compassionate while quietly closing the door. "I am scattered" may feel kinder than "I failed," but it still predicts the next failure if nothing in the scene changes. Finn's arborist report is a better test. The truck, tablet, and storm photo give him a place to disprove the story without arguing with it. Three uploaded photos matter more than a new self-description.

Miriam's stagehand scene adds another angle. "Old-school means reliable" sounds like pride, yet it can hide from the cue software the show now needs. When she enters the first light cue herself, the identity shifts from old-school to dependable in the current room. The words follow the act, not the other way around.

Use this carefully. A different self-story should not become forced optimism. It should be a claim small enough to verify today: careful pilot, observant beekeeper, reliable treasurer, tree-risk professional. If the behavior happens, the story gets evidence.
